tldr: By keeping the internal predictive states of a pretrained robotic world model (VLA-JEPA) frozen and adding a tiny readout head with only 34k parameters, FARM achieves accurate and causal task failure detection.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of FARM. Predictive state tokens are extracted from a frozen VLA-JEPA, routed through a shared linear projection, attention pooling, and a small MLP (totalling 33,985 parameters) to compute step-wise failure scores, and the cumulative maximum yields causal trajectory risk.
overview:
When robots perform autonomous tasks, failing to realize that an error has occurred leads to pointless actions or even physical damage to the environment. However, conventional error detection systems have either relied on proxy signals like action uncertainty or novelty—which do not directly reflect failure—or required training massive, dedicated monitoring models from scratch.

To address this, the authors focused on an intuitive question: "Do the internal predictive states of a robotic world model, trained to anticipate next states and action effects, already naturally contain failure signals?" If so, one should not need to fine-tune the heavy world model at all; simply extracting its internal representations and lightly decoding them should suffice.

FARM was developed to test this hypothesis. FARM extracts predictive state vectors from the 12th block of a frozen robotic world model (VLA-JEPA) and scores failure severity at each step through a tiny readout layer of just 33,985 parameters. In evaluations across 10 tasks in the LIBERO benchmark, FARM outperformed 15 matched baselines to achieve the highest Seen performance. Across three different real-robot setups (PIPER X, SO-101, and Franka) and unseen policies, it successfully captured failures either zero-shot or with minimal adaptation. Adding only 0.23 ms of mean CUDA latency on a GPU, FARM provides an exceptionally practical solution ready for real-world deployment.
contributions: Formulated robot failure monitoring as a lightweight readout problem from the internal predictive states of a frozen world model.
Proposed FARM, which computes step-wise failure scores and causal risk using a tiny 33,985-parameter readout layer without updating the backbone at all.

Demonstrated superior failure detection over prior baselines, real-robot transferability, and an ultra-low latency of 0.23 ms across 10 simulation tasks and 3 real-robot environments with 4 policy setups.

sections.heading: Why is failure monitoring hard, and why look at world models?
sections.summary: Even as vision policies like VLAs advance, robots still confidently execute failures. Unlike conventional monitors based on uncertainty or novelty, this work asks whether failure signals already sleep inside the internal states of predictive world models.
sections.details:
The emergence of vision-language-action models (VLAs: models that directly generate robot actions from images and text instructions) and generative policies has significantly expanded robotic capabilities. However, long-horizon real-world deployment demands not just action generation, but monitoring whether the execution is currently failing. Minor compounding errors or familiar actions leading to unexpected physical outcomes can cause a policy to freeze or stall while remaining highly confident.

Prior work has explored human-in-the-loop intervention frameworks (like HG-DAgger) and automated monitors that track model uncertainty, novelty, or action consistency. Yet these do not strictly equate to failure. An observation might look visually novel while the task succeeds, or the robot might fail repeatedly with high confidence.

On the other hand, noting the success of reading task outcomes from policy features (SAFE), one would expect world models—which integrate observation histories and physical predictions—to accumulate even richer failure information. This work explores whether failure signals can be directly decoded from the internal states of a predictive world model while keeping the pretrained backbone completely frozen.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of execution monitoring, world models, and feature reuse
sections.summary: This work builds on human intervention learning, statistical anomaly detection, recent latent world models for robotics, and probing techniques for frozen representations. Its novelty lies in reusing existing predictive states as fixed features rather than training world models dedicated to monitoring.
sections.details:
### II-A Execution Monitoring and Failure Signals
Robotic execution monitoring spans methods that leverage human interventions (such as HG-DAgger and Sirius) and automated scoring approaches that track uncertainty or temporal action consistency (such as FAIL-Detect, Sentinel, and FIPER). Recently, SAFE demonstrated success in classifying task outcomes using an MLP on VLA policy features. FARM shares SAFE's philosophy of representation reuse, but fundamentally differs by reading out from the predictive states of a world model rather than policy features.

### II-B Predictive World Models and Latent Representations
Starting with DreamerV3 and TD-MPC, robotics has seen significant progress in world models that simulate environmental transitions in compact latent spaces. Recent models predict in DINOv2 feature space (DINO-WM) or adopt Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs, which predict abstract future features rather than reconstructing raw pixels), such as V-JEPA 2 and VLA-JEPA. FARM preserves these predictive objectives and interrogates the richness of the representations they have already acquired.

### II-C World Models for Failure Monitoring
Prior monitoring methods leveraging world models (such as Foresight and FoMo-FD) co-train dynamics models specifically for monitoring or treat prediction errors directly as anomaly scores. In contrast, FARM keeps a general-purpose pretrained world model fixed and reuses it via a lightweight, linear probe (a small classifier designed to probe the information contained in internal representations).

sections.heading: Uncovering failures with just 34k parameters: the design of FARM
sections.summary: FARM takes predictive tokens from the final layer of a frozen VLA-JEPA, compresses them to 32 dimensions via shared projection and attention pooling, and outputs step-wise failure probabilities. Tracking the cumulative maximum yields causal, real-time trajectory risk without using future information.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Extracting Frozen World-Model States
FARM utilizes the predictor of a pretrained VLA-JEPA. The encoder and predictor parameters $\phi$ remain completely frozen. At replanning step $t$, the predictive tokens generated from the observation history are filtered to remove action-conditioning tokens, yielding the world-state tokens $H_{t}^{WM} \in \mathbb{R}^{768 \times 1024}$ (768 tokens with hidden dimension 1024). This corresponds to the raw output of the 12th block before normalization and output projection.

### III-C Ultra-Lightweight Failure Readout
Directly processing a large $768 \times 1024$ matrix with a high-capacity model would make it unclear whether the world model is informative or the detector simply learned the task on its own. FARM therefore adopts a strictly minimal architecture:
- Compresses each token from 1024 to 32 dimensions via a shared linear projection
- Applies LayerNorm and GELU, followed by attention pooling across the 768 tokens using a learned attention weight vector $a \in \mathbb{R}^{32}$
- Passes the pooled 32-dimensional vector through a small 1-layer MLP (32→32) to obtain the failure representation $z_t^F \in \mathbb{R}^{32}$
- Outputs a step score $s_t \in [0, 1]$ via a 1D linear head and a sigmoid function
The entire readout contains only 33,985 parameters. Attention operates strictly within the current time step, avoiding any temporal leakage.

### III-D & III-E Training Objective and Causal Risk Monitoring
Training uses task-balanced binary cross-entropy (BCE) to prevent data imbalance across tasks. The trajectory-level outcome label $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ is assigned as the target for each step.
During inference, causal risk is monitored by taking the running maximum of step scores: $q_t = \max_{\tau \le t} s_\tau$ (recursively $q_t = \max(q_{t-1}, s_t)$). Because it does not peek into future steps, it can be directly used online to halt the robot or trigger recovery behaviors.

### III-F Zero-Shot Transfer and Minimal Adaptation
FARM supports both zero-shot monitoring (applying weights $\theta$ learned in source environments directly to target settings) and Readout-Only Adaptation (fine-tuning only the 34k readout parameters using labeled target trajectories). In neither case are the world model parameters $\phi$ updated.

Predictive tokens ($768 \times 1024$) extracted from the frozen VLA-JEPA are aggregated into a 32-dimensional failure representation $z_t^F$ via shared token projection and attention pooling, yielding the step-wise failure score $s_t$ and cumulative maximum risk $q_t$.

sections.heading: Validation across 10 simulation tasks and 3 real-robot platforms
sections.summary: In simulation, FARM surpassed 15 baselines to achieve the highest Seen performance (AUROC 89.73). It also demonstrated high transferability and adaptability across real robots (PIPER X, SO-101, Franka), with an inference latency of just 0.23 ms on a GPU.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Effectiveness of Frozen Representations and Task Scaling
Evaluations were conducted on 10 tasks in the LIBERO benchmark (7 source training tasks S1–S7 and 3 strict unseen tasks U1–U3). First, compared to logistic regression baselines trained on simple world-model summary statistics (mean, variance, norm, across 7 stats), FARM achieved a substantially higher 85.68 AUROC / 88.59 AUPRC under 5-fold out-of-fold evaluation. Furthermore, scaling the training tasks from 1 to 7 monotonically improved Macro AUROC from 62.55% to 85.43%.

### IV-C Comparison with 15 Baselines
FARM was compared against 15 baselines, including policy-feature readouts like SAFE (MLP/LSTM), action variance, Mahalanobis distance, and flow-matching likelihood (LogpZO). On Seen tasks, FARM topped all methods with a Macro AUROC of 87.42, outperforming SAFE-MLP by 5.42 points. While STAC-Single (zero-shot action consistency) performed strongly on Strict-Unseen tasks, adapting only FARM's readout on a small budget of target data (Adapt-35) placed FARM at the top across all metrics.

### IV-D Real-Robot Transfer Experiments
Real-robot validation spanned 4 diverse setups differing in arm hardware and manipulation policies:
- PIPER X / $\pi^*_{0.6}$ (external policy, plug insertion, etc.)
- PIPER X / VLA-JEPA (autonomous policy, duck toy manipulation)
- SO-101 / Eval-RL (RL policy, blue cube grasping)
- Franka / $\pi_0$-FAST-DROID (public dataset, 13 tasks, 778 rollouts)
In all environments, FARM's step score $s_t$ exhibited a sharp rise at the exact moment of failure. Furthermore, FARM-Adapt (adapting only the readout layer on target data) achieved 75.78 AUROC / 74.31 AUPRC across all Franka data, demonstrating strong adaptability.

### IV-E Causal Monitoring and Ultra-Low Latency
When evaluated on partial trajectory histories at 25%, 50%, and 75% progress, FARM reached nearly its full performance (81.63 AUROC) by 75% completion. In terms of runtime measured on an RTX 5090, once the frozen world-model state is extracted, FARM's CUDA scoring latency averaged just 0.2256 ms (0.2393 ms at P99), achieving a throughput exceeding 4,432 steps/s. This allows seamless integration into existing robot control loops without overhead.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions
sections.summary: FARM shows that frozen world models enable highly accurate failure monitoring with just a tiny readout head. Future steps include investigating layer-wise failure localization and coupling detection scores with automated recovery policies.
sections.details:
Addressing the fundamental question of whether failure monitoring requires training a dedicated model from scratch, this work revealed that useful failure signals already exist within the internal states of pretrained world models. The proposed method, FARM, delivers excellent failure detection in both simulation and real-world setups with a 33,985-parameter readout layer without modifying the world model weights.

Limitations remain. Zero-shot transfer quality depends on source data diversity, and fully unseen tasks require target adaptation data. It also assumes access to the world model's internal tensors. Future directions include clarifying which predictor layers concentrate specific failure signals, and directly connecting the resulting risk scores to automated recovery behaviors for closed-loop correction.

takeaways: Robotic world models (VLA-JEPA) internally acquire representations that recognize whether a task is heading toward failure, beyond just predicting actions.
Without any backbone fine-tuning, training a tiny head of just 34k parameters outperforms heavy, dedicated monitoring baselines.
With an ultra-low CUDA latency of 0.23 ms (over 4,400 steps/s), it serves as a highly practical safety monitor and intervention trigger for real-time autonomous robots.
limitations: Requires an open architecture with direct access to internal world-model representations (tensors), making it inapplicable via black-box APIs.
Zero-shot transfer to completely unseen tasks (Strict-Unseen) has limitations, requiring a small budget of labeled adaptation trajectories (around several dozen) for optimal accuracy.
Developing specific recovery control algorithms that act on detected failure scores remains outside the scope of this paper.
